timeline.title: Congress creates the program
timeline.body: Section 3025 of the Affordable Care Act adds the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program to the Social Security Act, section 1886(q).

timeline.title: Penalties begin, capped at 1%
timeline.body: Three conditions count: heart attack, heart failure, and pneumonia.

timeline.title: Cap rises to 2%
timeline.body: The statute steps the maximum reduction up each year until it reaches 3%.

timeline.title: Cap reaches 3%; COPD and hip/knee replacement added
timeline.body: The 3% maximum is set in law and has not changed since.

src.label: FY2014 IPPS final rule, 78 FR 50663–50664 (COPD and hip/knee)

timeline.title: Bypass surgery added; pneumonia definition widened
timeline.body: The pneumonia group now includes aspiration pneumonia and sepsis with pneumonia present on admission.

src.label: Bypass: FY2015 IPPS final rule, 79 FR 50039. Pneumonia: FY2016 IPPS final rule, 80 FR 49532–49533

timeline.title: Congress orders peer comparisons
timeline.body: The 21st Century Cures Act requires CMS to compare each hospital with hospitals serving similar shares of patients who have both Medicare and full Medicaid.

src.label: 21st Century Cures Act, Pub. L. 114-255, sec. 15002

timeline.title: Peer grouping starts
timeline.body: Hospitals are sorted into five peer groups by dual-eligible share and judged against their group's median. A neutrality modifier keeps total penalties the same as the old method.

timeline.title: COVID-19: early-2020 data set aside
timeline.body: A CMS memo dated this day excludes claims from January through June 2020. The gap shows up in the FY2022 through FY2024 calculations.

timeline.title: Pneumonia sits out a year
timeline.body: CMS suppresses the pneumonia measure for FY2023 and removes COVID-19 patients from the other measures.

timeline.title: Pneumonia returns
timeline.body: Patients with a COVID-19 diagnosis stay out of every measure through FY2026.

src.label: FY2023 IPPS final rule; end date: FY2026 IPPS final rule, 90 FR 36930

timeline.title: Medicare Advantage patients counted; two-year window
timeline.body: Adopted in the FY2026 rule: readmission ratios now include Medicare Advantage patients, the data window shrinks from three years to two, and the COVID-19 exclusion ends. The cut still applies only to traditional Medicare payments.

timeline.title: Next: sepsis
timeline.body: The FY2027 rule adds a seventh measure, readmission after sepsis. Hospitals get confidential reports for FY2028 and FY2029; it counts toward penalties starting FY2030.

research.title: Readmissions, Observation, and the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program
research.finding: Readmissions for the targeted conditions fell from 21.5% to 17.8% between 2007 and 2015. Observation stays grew, but hospitals with bigger readmission drops did not show bigger observation growth.

research.title: Association Between Hospital Penalty Status Under the HRRP and Readmission Rates for Target and Nontarget Conditions
research.finding: Hospitals that were later penalized cut readmissions faster than others after the program was announced. The improvement leveled off once penalties began in October 2012.

research.title: Mandated report: The effects of the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program
research.finding: Congress's advisers concluded the program lowered readmissions without a material rise in ER visits, observation stays, or deaths, saving Medicare roughly $1.5 billion a year by 2016. They suggested accounting for hospitals' low-income patient share.

research.cite: Ibrahim et al., JAMA Intern Med 2018
research.title: Association of Coded Severity With Readmission Reduction After the HRRP
research.finding: In this research letter, about 63% of the risk-adjusted decline was statistically attributable to rising coded severity at exposed hospitals. The authors could not tell whether the coding change was appropriate.

research.cite: Sabbatini et al., JAMA Netw Open 2022
research.title: Accounting for the Growth of Observation Stays in the Assessment of Medicare's HRRP
research.finding: Counting observation stays as returns cut the measured drop for targeted conditions from 1.48 to 0.66 points. The program's extra effect over non-targeted conditions was no longer statistically significant.

research.cite: Wright et al., Health Serv Res 2023
research.title: Medicare's hospital readmissions reduction program and the rise in observation stays
research.finding: Observation use rose only slightly faster for targeted conditions after the program began; most of the growth tracked other forces, such as billing audits.

research.title: Decreases In Readmissions Credited To Medicare's Program To Reduce Hospital Readmissions Have Been Overstated
research.finding: A change in billing standards at the same time let hospitals list more diagnoses per claim, which lowered risk-adjusted readmission rates. Accounting for it cut the measured decline for targeted conditions by 48%, and after further adjustment that decline matched two control groups.

research.title: Association of HRRP Implementation With Readmission and Mortality Outcomes in Heart Failure
research.finding: In a registry of 416 participating hospitals, with a before/after comparison and no control group, 30-day readmissions fell from 20.0% to 18.4% while 30-day deaths rose from 7.2% to 8.6% after penalties began. The authors called for confirmation.

research.title: Association of the HRRP With Mortality Among Medicare Beneficiaries Hospitalized for Heart Failure, AMI, and Pneumonia
research.finding: Across 8.3 million hospitalizations, deaths within 30 days after discharge rose for heart failure and pneumonia, mostly among patients who were never readmitted, and fell for heart attack. Deaths within 45 days of admission did not change significantly. The authors called for more research.

research.cite: Khera et al., JAMA Netw Open 2018
research.title: Association of the HRRP With Mortality During and After Hospitalization for AMI, Heart Failure, and Pneumonia
research.finding: Looking at the same three conditions, this team found no change in mortality trends when the program was announced or started. Heart failure deaths after discharge were already rising before the program.

research.title: Association of Changing Hospital Readmission Rates With Mortality Rates After Hospital Discharge
research.finding: In a hospital-level study of Medicare patients with heart failure, heart attack, or pneumonia from 2008 to 2014, hospitals whose readmissions fell tended to see deaths after discharge fall too, though the link was weak. The authors said this does not support rising deaths from cutting readmissions.

research.theme: Is it fair to safety-net hospitals?
research.cite: Joynt Maddox et al., JAMA Intern Med 2019
research.title: Association of Stratification by Dual Enrollment Status With Financial Penalties in the HRRP
research.finding: Comparing actual FY2018 and FY2019 penalties, the peer-group change cut penalties about $22 million for hospitals with the most dual-eligible patients and raised them about $12 million for those with the fewest.

research.theme: Is it fair to safety-net hospitals?
research.title: Three-Year Impact Of Stratification In The Medicare HRRP
research.finding: After three years, peer grouping lowered penalties modestly at hospitals with many dual-eligible, rural, Black, or Hispanic patients. The authors called it a modest step toward equity.

research.cite: Oseran et al., Ann Intern Med 2023
research.title: Effect of Medicare Advantage on Hospital Readmission and Mortality Rankings
research.finding: When Medicare Advantage patients were added to the measures, about one in four top-ranked hospitals dropped to a lower rank, while a similar share of the lowest-ranked rose. Hospitals with more Medicare Advantage patients tended to improve. Under CMS's FY2026 rule, FY2027 is the first payment year built this way.

research.cite: Chopra et al., JAMA Netw Open 2026
research.title: Hospital Readmission Reduction Program Penalties for Hospitals With High Medicare Advantage Penetration
research.finding: Using FY2019–FY2022 data, adjusting for local Medicare Advantage enrollment would have shifted roughly $284–297 million a year in penalties among hospitals.
